title: You have an array of `n` numbers that should hold each value `1..n` exactly once, but due to corruption one number got duplicated which caused another number to go missing. Return the pair `[duplicate, missing]` in O(n) time and O(1) space.
shortTitle: Find the Corrupt Pair (One Duplicate and One Missing in 1..n)
keyPoints: After Cyclic Sort placement, exactly one slot has value != index+1; its stored value is the duplicate and index+1 is the missing number.
The duplicate-safe value-comparison guard prevents infinite swaps when the duplicate reaches its home.
One placement pass plus one scan: O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
The algebraic alternative uses sum and sum-of-squares differences to solve two equations for two unknowns, but risks overflow for large n.
Cyclic Sort is overflow-free and more readable, making it the preferred interview answer.
This problem combines Find the Duplicate and Find the Missing into a single unified Cyclic Sort application.

s1_definition.oneliner: After cyclic placement, the one mismatched slot gives the duplicate (its value) and the missing (its index+1) together.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Corrupt Pair** – an array of n values in 1..n has one duplicate and one missing; return both.
- **Cyclic Sort** – place each value v at index v-1; after placement, exactly one slot is mismatched.
- **Mismatched slot** – the stored value is the duplicate, and index+1 is the missing number.
- **Algebraic alternative** – use the difference of sums and squared sums to solve for both, but risks overflow.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India keeps one ledger page per number 1 to n, but a copying error duplicated one page number and therefore dropped another. A clerk files each page at its slot. The single stranded slot tells both the page number that was copied twice and the page number that vanished.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the corrupt pair, where one number is duplicated and that duplication forced another number to go missing, is one of the most satisfying Cyclic Sort applications because a single placement pass surrenders both answers at once. I place each value at the index equal to the value minus one with the duplicate-safe guard, and because exactly one value is doubled and exactly one is absent, precisely one slot ends up mismatched. At that slot the stored value is the duplicate and the index plus one is the missing number.

I know the algebraic approach using the difference of sums and squared sums also recovers both unknowns, but it risks overflow for large n and reads less clearly, so Cyclic Sort is my preferred interview answer. The XOR-based approach is a third option that avoids overflow but is the hardest to explain.

This problem is the natural combination of Find the Duplicate and Find the Missing into a single unified Cyclic Sort application. Recognising that unification is what makes it elegant and quick to code.

In my work at the National Bank of India, this backed a ledger integrity audit. The ledger assigned each entry a page number in a known range, and a copy fault occasionally duplicated one page number while dropping another. Placing every page at its home index then reporting the single mismatched slot delivered both numbers in linear time and constant space.

Remember one sentence: after Cyclic Sort, the one mismatched slot gives both the duplicate (its stored value) and the missing (its index+1) in a single O(n) pass.
